Why would they not? I mean, like, if you go and win an event and then
refuse to give out a deck list, there really isn't anything anyone can
do about it ("Hey, Bill, can I get a deck list of your winning deck?"
"Uhh, ok, I'll, uhh, get right on that...") But as giving out your deck

Messages.Body:

To make one thing absolutely clear: We checked the decklists of the
finalists. They were all correct.

In Germany all things you create are your "geistiges Eigentum" and are
protected by Copyright. As LSJ stated above you give that right away
by entering a tournament. So I know that it's perfectly legal to post
the finalist's lists. But for me decklists are somewhat sensible
information. So if somebody asks (begs) me to don't publish it for
some reasons shouldn't I respect that?
Until now I were always proud of my winning decks and wanted everybody
to know of it. I always wrote stories of how they did in tournaments.
I always enjoy reading other's lists and think that many players may
improve and learn by playing decks created with that help. That is why
the attitude of keeping lists secret is totally new for me.
Nonetheless I'd like to accept and honour it.

Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
"Wolflord" <jo.her...@sca.com> wrote in
news:1172690521.2...@z35g2000cwz.googlegroups.com:



Then you should know that you are also disagreeing with the VEKN Judge's
Guidelines. There are seperate sections of the Penalty Guide for dealing
with Deck List Variances (section 100) and Cheating (section 160). The
VEKN doesn't conflate the two, and neither should you. A decklist variant
should not be automatically assumed to be cheating, as the "philosophy"
section of 101, 102 and 103 details;

101 Illegal Decklist
Philosophy:

The decklist is the ultimate guide to a player's deck. If the decklist
lists an illegal deck, the player is playing with an illegal deck,
regardless of the actual contents of his or her deck. However, it is not in
the best interest of the event to disqualify players for illegal decklists.

Penalty: Warning

102. Deck Problem - Illegal Main Deck (Legal Decklist)
Philosophy:

The decklist is the ultimate guide to a player's deck. If the decklist
indicates a legal deck, but the actual contents of the deck do not match
the decklist, the player should restore the deck to reflect the decklist.
If the judge can determine with complete confidence that the deck/decklist
discrepancy is due to an error on the decklist (a player is using an all
Gangrel deck and has Campground Hunting Ground listed on the decklist
instead of Zoo Hunting Ground), he or she may decide to fix the decklist
instead. A warning should be issued in this case.

Penalty: Game Loss

103. Deck Problem - Illegal Main Deck (No Decklist Used)

Philosophy:

If the deck contains an illegal selection of cards in some manner, the
player is playing with an illegal deck. However, it is not in the best
interest of the event to disqualify players for illegal decks.

Penalty: Game Loss

Compare how those read to, say, Section 163, which is what you seem to be
implying that you are "catching" with illegal decklists...

163. Cheating - Fraud
Definition:
A player intentionally misrepresents rules, procedures, personal
information, or any other relevant tournament information.

Example:
A player uses a fake name and V:EKN number when registering for a
tournament.

Philosophy:
There should be zero tolerance for this type of activity.

Penalty:
Disqualification without Prize.

full text for the Judges Guide is here;

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/index.php?line=veknjudgesguide

> You are the one claiming the most common mistakes in decklists are due
> to people making simple mistakes while writing them, rather then
> attempts at cheating.

No, you are the one conflating cheating and deck list issues, and more
importantly your interpretation isn't supported by the VEKN Judge's Guide.
A Deck List variance may be an indicator of the possiblity cheating, but it
is not conclusive proof, nor is it cheating in and of itself. If it were,
deck list variances would be in the Judge's Guide as examples under 163,
rather than getting a seperate section to themselves.

> If you have such faith in players in general, the you're simply

> extremely naďve.

If you're applying 163 when you should be applying 101, 102, or 103, then
you're simply being a bad Judge.

> Also, give me 1 reason why checking for marked cards in a deck would
> not be part of checking a deck/deklist?
>

These are two different activities. The fact that they cna be done
simultaneously doesn't change that fact. Marked Cards have their own
section in the Penalty Guide, as well, Section 130 (again, _not_ a sub-
section of Cheating). I think you might be well served by a read through
the whole document. It seems that you are confusing what you are actually
catching and penalizing as a Judge...

Regards
DaveZ
Atom Weaver

Messages.Author: Jay Kristoff

"Wolflord" wrote:

>It comes down to this: cheating is really really easy.
>Changing the "meaningless statistics" of your deck over
>the course of a tournament,or pazcking a deck which
>simply does not fit within the boundaries set by the rules
>is about the easiest way to increase your own chances of
>winning. Checking deck prevents just that activity.

The time when changing cards would be most effective
is before a final round; as a finalist may have an idea about
what some of his competitors are playing. Changing one's
deck in between preliminary rounds seems silly and futile,
even if you have a print out of the Archon's optimal seating
chart. With that in mind, I recommend that if there is going
to be a break before the final round of a tournament, then
the judge should simply hold the finalists' decks until the
final round begins (instead of collecting and checking decklists).
I think this policy thwarts the most effective type of cheating
and prevents players from being ejected for having poor clarical
skills.

Jay Kristoff, V:EKN Prince of Columbus, Ohio USA

I didn´t investigate the reasons behind the errors, I pointed them out
to the players, applied the penalty and moved on. Perhaps I would not
have applied the game-loss in the Atonement case if there hadn´t been
the other case.

Yes, in retrospect I have certainly learned from the experience and
would do it differently now. That I had 100+F° fever this day certainly
didn´t help nor the fact that I was very exhausted from the day where we
had problems with certain players and we needed to get the finals going.

That should not be an excuse for the decision since I still think it can
be justified, it´s just to show people that running 100+ player events
is physically and mentally exhausting. Time pressure is usually quite
high (and in return we were praised for running the whole event with a
total delay < 15 min) and I was not prepared for that kind of situation.

That tells me that we should have some better guidelines for judges with
good examples from the reality of those people who have experienced
though judging environments. We should also think about rewarding the
judges in big events since it is really a difficult and demanding job.
Not to forget that you forfeit the chance to play.

Johannes
